$comment: The per-tool MCP permission ladder, stated once for every reader of it.
Three codebases read this ladder and each one used to be tested only against its own
restatement of it: the Python SDK (MCPPolicy.resolved_new_tool_permission and to_wire in
sdks/python/agenta/sdk/agents/mcp/models.py), the runner
(normalizeMcpServerPermissions and mcpToolPermission in services/runner/src/mcp-permission.ts),
and the web editor (resolvedNewToolPermission and effectiveToolPermission in
web/packages/agenta-entities/src/mcpEndpoint/core/toolPolicy.ts, read through policyAdapter.ts).
That is how D88 shipped: every suite was green while two readers disagreed about whether the
whole-server permission is the floor for a tool a per-tool table does not name. It is not.
The three answers chain rather than merely resembling one another. `wire` is what the SDK
emits for `policy`, and it is the runner's input, so a case is only green when the SDK's
output is the thing the runner resolves. The web reads `policy` directly, because the editor
edits the saved shape.
`null` in an expectation means NO DECISION: the reader defers, and the caller's own ladder
(rules, then the run default) decides exactly as it did before per-tool policy existed.
Add a case here before changing any of the three readers. A case with `namedTool` null has no
Add a case here before changing any of the three readers. A case with `namedTool` null has no
per-tool table, so there is no named tool to resolve.
`sendersThatOmitTheFloor` is the runner's alone. The SDK resolves the floor before it emits,
so every `wire` above carries `newToolPermission` and the runner's own fallback branch is
unreachable from this SDK. A hand-written sender and an older one do reach it, and it is the
branch D88 lived in, so the shapes they send are stated here too.

cases.name: absent
cases.why: No policy at all. Every reader defers, and this is what every configuration written before per-tool policy looks like.

cases.name: server allow, no table
cases.why: The whole-server permission governs every tool while no table is declared.

cases.name: server allow plus one deny
cases.why: D88 itself. A table with no floor beside it asks for anything it does not name, and `permission: allow` does NOT reach those tools. Reading it as the floor sent newToolPermission allow and ran unnamed tools unapproved.

cases.name: server allow plus one deny plus new tool allow
cases.why: Decision 38: an author who wants an open server with one hole says so explicitly, and then unnamed tools really do run.

cases.name: server ask plus read-only tools allow plus new tool ask
cases.why: Decision 45: the read-only preset. The named reads run unattended and everything else reaches a human, including a tool the server starts advertising later.

cases.name: table only
cases.why: Opting in through the table alone. No whole-server permission exists to be mistaken for the floor, so the `ask` floor is the only thing that can answer an unnamed tool.

cases.name: new tool only
cases.why: Opting in through the floor alone, with nothing named yet. Every advertised tool takes the floor.

sendersThatOmitTheFloor.name: server allow, table declared, floor omitted
sendersThatOmitTheFloor.why: The branch D88 lived in. A human decides for anything the table does not name, and `permission: allow` is not that decision.

sendersThatOmitTheFloor.name: server deny, table declared, floor omitted
sendersThatOmitTheFloor.why: The same floor in the other direction: `ask` is not read off `permission` when that would be stricter either, or a reader could not tell the two apart.
